prize_parts.citation: for credibly identified evidence on how import competition and technology reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My names and ballot are unchanged from round 1, but I have narrowed the citation. It now rests on the identified evidence and no longer claims the task framework as a whole. B032 is the candidate where I see data discovery and an explanatory framework most clearly together. The shift-share exposure design applied to local labour markets is a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution. It turned a broad question about who bears the costs of trade and technology into something that can be measured, challenged and re-estimated. The core papers date from about 2003 to 2016, so the work has been through years of scrutiny. The qualitative findings are that adjustment is slow, that exposed workers and places bear persistent costs, and that these costs are distributed unevenly. These findings have held up in follow-on work even though magnitudes are still debated. I have not changed my view on merit or maturity. Round 1 did not give me a reason to move to another candidate, and I do not treat the fact that three positions have equal explicit backing as evidence about which is best. I weigh attribution cleanliness, identification credibility and durability, and on those criteria I still find B032 the most defensible, with real costs that I state below.
statement.case_against: The attribution costs are real. The task-based theory also rests on people outside this ballot (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo), so a narrower, evidence-centred citation is the honest way to credit this work. Katz's skill-premium and education-technology work is a distinct foundational strand, and leaving him out is a genuine loss that I do not want to understate. The aggregate magnitude and long-run persistence of the China shock are still contested, and so is the inference for exposure-based designs. Recent labour and technology recognition (Card, Angrist and Imbens, Goldin, Acemoglu 2024) could lead the Committee to see this area as already well covered. I think the overlap is partial. Those prizes concerned gender gaps, natural experiments on minimum wages and immigration, and institutions and prosperity, not trade and technology shocks to labour demand. But that is a judgement, and members can reasonably weigh it differently.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B016 first. He calls B032 the most serious competing case and treats it as a real alternative. If B032 were chosen he would keep Dorn with Autor and Hanson rather than Katz, because the credited achievement is local labour-market evidence on import competition. He thinks the task framework is partly owed to people outside the list.
responses.response: I agree with the Dorn-over-Katz logic. It is also why I narrowed the citation to evidence on import competition and technology shocks to labour demand, so that it does not appear to claim the whole task framework. We part ways on the comparison. I do not think B016's credit line is cleaner once I weigh identification. You rest B016 on the formal framework and on later sharper designs, which is a fair argument. But for the constitutional-effects evidence, B032's designs are more directly checkable. B016's overlap with the 2024 institutions prize is also more material than any overlap I see for B032. I would not oppose a B016 prize if the citation carried the identification caveats you accept. Besley is the contestable name in that trio, and a two-person award would be cleaner.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B010 first and lists B032 as a serious alternative. He argues that the tasks and skill premium (Autor, Katz) and the China shock (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) are two strands combined under a three-name cap. He wants the Committee to decide which strand it honours before choosing names, and he would lean to Autor and Hanson plus Dorn or Katz accordingly.
responses.response: This is the right sequencing and I have tried to follow it. My answer is that the Committee honours one strand, the identified evidence on how trade and technology shocks reshape labour demand and local adjustment, and that the citation says so. On that reading Dorn is the third name, because the local labour-market design is a joint product of the three. If the Committee wanted the tasks and skill-premium strand, Katz would become the natural third name, but then the citation would have to credit Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo's lineage in background, and I would not support that wording on this ballot. I do not claim the choice is free of cost, since Katz's work is foundational. I keep Dorn because I can attribute the evidence strand cleanly to three people.

responses.point: Andersson now ranks B014 first and keeps B032 as an alternative. He regards B032 as more policy-salient but more debated, because the China-shock magnitudes are contested and task-framework credit extends beyond the credited names. He prefers a citation that avoids overclaiming on forecasting performance for B014.
responses.response: I accept the debate over magnitude and the credit point, and I would put the weight on what I think is robust: the qualitative local adjustment findings, not any single aggregate number. On the chair's question about maturity, my recollection, which I have not independently verified here, is that the exposure designs have been re-examined. This includes the inference literature on shift-share designs (for example Adão, Kolesár and Morales, and Borusyak, Hull and Jaravel), and the authors' own later work on the persistence of the China shock. The persistent local costs have generally survived, while the size of employment effects and the speed of adjustment remain debated. That is why I frame the citation around evidence and not around a number. On B014, I agree that it has a large policy footprint and I keep it as an alternative. Your point about the baseline model's post-2021 performance affects wording and not the contribution. My hesitation remains that eight credited names make any trio contestable.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B010 first and B032 second. She calls the China-shock evidence among the most credible quasi-experimental work on the list and says the cleanest B032 credit line is Autor, Hanson and Dorn, with the task theory depending on Acemoglu and Restrepo. She holds B010 first because its credit line is slightly easier to defend.
responses.response: We agree on the B032 names and on the incompleteness of the task-theory credit. Where we differ is the attribution comparison. B010 has a tidy pair, but Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are uncredited, and the quantitative welfare gains rest on functional-form choices. B032 has a three-person unit that I think is the natural co-authored core of its evidence. Its uncredited contributors sit mostly on the theory side, which a narrow citation can leave out. On measurement I give the transparent reduced-form designs more weight than a model whose headline welfare effects depend on parametrisation. I accept that this is a judgement about weighting and not a decisive scientific difference. I would not oppose B010 on scientific grounds. If the Committee decides the cleanest listed credit pair matters most, then B010 is a defensible choice.

responses.point: Teorell moved from B042 first to B032 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He weights transparent designs that have survived re-examination, and he gives the persistence critiques and the thematic proximity to recent prizes as the main reasons for caution. He keeps B042 as his first alternative with a tight two-person credit line.
responses.response: I agree with his reasoning and with the narrowing to Dorn. I share his view that B042's attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, and that is why it remains my first alternative. We both weight the gap between theoretical influence and direct identification of the collateral channel, and I would stay with the Kiyotaki-Moore pair and not add Gertler if the Committee chose B042. I would add one point about overlap. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is a closer neighbour to B042 than any recent prize is to B032, so I think B032 carries less timing risk on that dimension. That difference is not large and I would not call B042 disqualified.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the identified trade-shock and technology evidence as a single achievement distinct from the task framework, and whether a narrowly worded citation is enough to handle the credit owed to Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo.

Dorn versus Katz for the third name. I have chosen Dorn on attribution grounds, but a Committee that wants the skill-premium strand would reasonably choose Katz. I would then want the citation to say so.

The long-run magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects and the validity of shift-share inference. My recollection of the re-examination literature is from memory, not independent source verification, and I may be missing recent work.

How far recent labour-market and technology recognition (Card, Angrist and Imbens, Goldin, Acemoglu 2024) reduces the case for B032. These prize facts are my own recollection and the Committee may weigh the overlap differently.

What would change my view: evidence that the local-adjustment findings fail under alternative inference and specification, or a Committee consensus that the task and skill-premium strand is the achievement to honour. In the latter case I would reconsider both the third name and my ranking against B042 and B014.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the credited B032 names (Autor, Hanson, Dorn, Katz) appears among my listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler). I disclose field proximity: I am a labour economist and sit on the editorial board of the American Economic Review, where work in this area is published. My ERC project on the inequality-crime cycle is thematically adjacent to the distributional costs of economic shocks. My 2023 committee entry coincided with the Goldin prize, and Katz is a Goldin co-author, which I flag because Katz is on the ballot but outside my configuration. These are disclosures and not adjudicated conflicts, and I applied common criteria.
